own_list: An attacker who obtains the password taped under a branch desk can impersonate desk staff using the shared circulation login and make unauthorized loan extensions, clear account blocks or mark unreturned books as returned. The same credential is used at every branch.

A dishonest desk worker can deliberately mark a book returned when it was not, clear a justified account block or grant an improper extension through the circulation page, corrupting loan records using their existing staff access.

A desk worker can deny making a fraudulent manual return, and investigators cannot attribute it to a person or branch: all staff share one account and the history records only that the loan was closed by hand.

An internet attacker could submit borrowing, renewal or reservation requests without a valid member identity if the lending API fails to authenticate requests or accepts invalid sign-in credentials. The API is internet-facing; Priya could not confirm what authentication it actually enforces, so this threat is conditional.

An authenticated member could change the member identifier in an app request to renew another member's loans or place reservations in their name if the API does not bind the requested member to the authenticated identity. Requests explicitly supply both book and member; checking loan rules does not establish this authorization check.

A member or unauthenticated caller could invoke staff-only manual-return, block-clearing or extension operations directly on the lending API if it fails to enforce staff authorization on those operations. The same API serves the circulation page and internet app traffic; endpoint access restrictions and role checks are not described.

A person using another member's borrowed, stolen or copied library card could borrow books against that member's account at a self-service kiosk if scanning the card is sufficient to establish identity. Card scanning is stated, but any additional identity check is unknown.

An attacker able to reach the kiosk-facing API operations could forge kiosk loan or return submissions, including falsely recording a return, if the API does not authenticate kiosks and authorize their operations. Kiosk-to-API authentication is unknown; branch-network placement alone does not establish a trusted caller.

An attacker could flood the internet-facing lending API with requests and exhaust its capacity, preventing borrowing and returns across phones and branches. Ordinary challenge-launch traffic has already taken the single service down twice, and there is no queue in front of it; the effectiveness of any rate limits is unknown.

An attacker positioned on a service communication path could capture member information or circulation credentials if that connection lacks effective transport encryption. Member, kiosk, staff and database connections have unknown transport protection; this is a conditional disclosure threat, not a claim that the service uses plaintext.

An attacker who obtains readable loans-database storage could disclose members' names, email addresses, home addresses and full borrowing histories if effective at-rest protection is absent. Storage encryption is unknown, so this is conditional on both storage access and missing protection.

model: process:lending-api exposure should be internet-facing, not unknown. Priya explicitly identifies the old internal-only statement as wrong and says phones now call the API directly over the internet. The note itself directs readers to her more recent account. This is an explicit correction, not an unresolved disagreement based only on recency.

model: store:loans-database data_classification is unknown even though the transcript explicitly identifies names, email addresses, home addresses and full borrowing histories, and the model itself already assigns the pii asset. Record the supported personal-data classification; an exact local sensitivity tier remains unspecified.
missing: A dishonest desk worker can deliberately mark an unreturned book returned, clear a justified account block or grant an improper loan extension using their existing circulation access, corrupting loan records. Row 20 gestures at these actions but asserts unsupported universal grants and misclassifies ordinary privilege misuse as escalation; row 11 covers stolen credentials and row 14 covers attribution, not this integrity threat.

A member or unauthenticated caller could invoke staff-only manual-return, block-clearing or extension operations if the lending API fails to enforce staff authorization on those endpoints. The API serves both circulation and app functions, but endpoint reachability and role checks are unknown. Row 19 describes reachability, not this conditional privilege-boundary failure.

A person using another member's borrowed, stolen or copied library card could borrow against that account at a self-service kiosk if card scanning is sufficient to establish identity. Additional identity checks are unknown. Row 10 concerns impersonating the kiosk to the API, not impersonating a member at a genuine kiosk.

An attacker on a staff-to-API, kiosk-to-API or API-to-database communication path could capture circulation credentials or member data carried there if effective transport encryption is absent. Transport protection is unknown on each flow. Rows 5 and 17 address only the phone-to-API path; row 16 addresses storage.
16-library-lending-interview.notes:
Sitting held as CSV in conversation. The own list was written before the recorded sets were opened. Row numbers refer to the marks ballot, one row per finding.
model: Confirm own-list entry 12 as a correction. Set lending API exposure to internet-facing. The note identifies itself as old and points to Priya for the current picture; Priya explicitly calls internal-only 'one of the wrong bits' and states that phones now talk directly to the API over the internet. This is explicit supersession, not recency alone resolving equally current conflicting claims. Update model.json and the corresponding facts.json assertion to preserve this correction and its provenance. Revise E1 (marks row 19): exposure alone is not elevation of privilege; do not retain an unknown-exposure finding solely to satisfy the trap. Public circulation-endpoint access remains unestablished.
model: Confirm own-list entry 13 as a correction. The loans database contains personal data: names, email addresses, home addresses and full borrowing histories. Record the supported personal-data classification consistently with the existing pii asset. The precise local sensitivity tier and at-rest encryption remain unknown; do not infer either.
Marking convention: ASVS 'agree' accepts the stated source-supported fact or evidence gap, not proven nonconformance or an independently verified requirement-ID mapping. For conditional STRIDE agreements, the stated control must actually be ineffective for the attack to follow. Silence or a hedge is not evidence that a control is absent. Keep those conditions explicit in final finding text.
Coverage: Shared evidence alone does not make two claims duplicates. A control-evidence question, a concrete attack and inability to attribute that attack can be distinct. Missing entries identify gaps in the submitted rows as written; the suggested rewrites of rows 19 and 20 would cover the corresponding missing entries without adding duplicates.
Reader's note on each row:
Row 1 (v5:6b106dfad813aa26, asvs V8.2.1): agree. The shared identity prevents person-specific authorization using that login alone. It does not imply that role-based access rules are impossible, or establish a particular ASVS compliance result.
Row 2 (v5:daf4c18d50d7dbc3, asvs V8.2.2): agree. An evidence gap: the API must bind the supplied member identifier and target records to the authenticated member. The sources do not establish whether it does.
Row 3 (v5:897184152b3bf29e, asvs V8.1.1): reject. The lending service note explicitly says desk staff may extend a loan, clear a block or mark a book returned; the transcript confirms those staff functions. A formal or sufficiently detailed authorization policy is not supplied, but 'No document says who may' is contradicted by the supplied note.
Row 4 (v5:7b85b051c409c13e, asvs V7.2.1): agree. Token verification is unconfirmed. Priya's tentative recollection is a lead to investigate, not a verified authentication mechanism and not proof that verification is absent.
Row 5 (v5:247a95563542d1b0, asvs V12.2.1): agree. Transport protection is unspecified. REST and JSON establish neither TLS nor plaintext.
Row 6 (v5:3ef7bcb24cedcabb, asvs V6.1.1): agree. Repeated sign-in protections are not described. This is a documentation/evidence gap, not proof that attempt limits are absent.
Row 7 (v5:982b91e50f170fbf, asvs V2.2.2): agree. Server-side validation of kiosk loan/return submissions is not established. The app walkthrough mentions loan-rule checks, but does not settle checks for kiosk submissions. Input/business validation is distinct from authenticating a kiosk in row 10.
Row 8 (v5:2e2ac850137a110c, asvs V1.2.4): agree. Query construction is unspecified. Database technology is also unspecified; this does not establish SQL usage, injection susceptibility or a failed control.
Row 9 (v6:9c78d0a74ddfb21d, stride spoofing): reject. Rewrite: If the internet-facing API fails to authenticate app requests, an attacker could borrow, renew or reserve as another member. Authentication is unknown, not known absent. The app flow does not establish an ability to end loans; manual closure and kiosk returns are separate operations.
Row 10 (v6:43611ef59e949638, stride spoofing): agree. Conditional: an attacker able to reach the kiosk operations could forge loan/return submissions if kiosk identity and operation authorization are ineffective. Unknown authentication does not prove that such submissions are accepted; 'any member' depends on additional authorization checks.
Row 11 (v6:b1b64873088d879f, stride spoofing): agree. Supported credential-disclosure and staff-impersonation path. It requires access to the password card; neither public access behind the desk nor internet access to the circulation page is established.
Row 12 (v6:336ca80c3e8411b1, stride tampering): agree. Conditional on absent or ineffective authenticated transport protection and an attacker on the path. Unknown encryption alone is not proof of modifiable traffic.
Row 13 (v6:4421d269123a1381, stride tampering): reject. Unknown API-to-database authentication does not establish an attacker-accessible database write path or bypass of database authorization. The stated architecture gives database access only to the API. Direct writes could be a conditional threat after specifying how an attacker obtains database connectivity and write authority; the rationale does not supply that mechanism.
Row 14 (v6:f5ec18a8ae0e9ba2, stride repudiation): agree. Supported lack of attribution to an individual or branch. The exact history wording is established for manual loan closure; the same shared identity also undermines attribution of other desk actions.
Row 15 (v6:2d8887ea000fd591, stride repudiation): reject. Unknown caller authentication does not establish that nothing can contradict a denial: audit records and other evidence are unspecified. Rewrite as a question about individual caller attribution and trustworthy records of renewals/reservations, rather than a demonstrated repudiation failure.
Row 16 (v6:efc2b4d2cd862582, stride information-disclosure): agree. Conditional on an attacker obtaining readable storage or a copy and effective at-rest protection being absent. Encryption at rest does not by itself stop a live database session with authorized read access. No accessible backup/copy is established.
Row 17 (v6:b34010ec17c1f9e7, stride information-disclosure): agree. Conditional on inadequate transport protection and an attacker on the path. Correct the rationale: the transcript explicitly corrects the old note, establishing internet access; the path is not uncertain because of that superseded note.
Row 18 (v6:bd6fd4c376ea7762, stride denial-of-service): agree. The observed overload outages support a credible availability threat from deliberate request flooding. A single service and no queue do not alone prove susceptibility; the two prior outages provide the stronger evidence. Rate limits and attacker load needed remain unknown.
Row 19 (v6:650104a35f760692, stride elevation-of-privilege): reject. Internet reachability is not elevation of privilege. Priya explicitly corrects the old internal-only statement, so API exposure is internet-facing, not unknown. Public API access also does not prove public access to circulation endpoints or bypass of staff authorization. See the missing threat about conditional access to staff-only operations.
Row 20 (v6:0f2ac7147862bbfe, stride elevation-of-privilege): reject. One shared login does not establish permission over every record in every branch or absence of all scoping/review. Staff already have the stated manual-change powers, so using them is not necessarily privilege escalation. Rewrite as deliberate staff misuse of those powers; stolen-login impersonation is already row 11 and deficient attribution is row 14.
